One neuron, one input, one update rule — the loop that every later model in the course is a scaled-up version of.

1958 — ROSENBLATT MSE · SGD · LEARNING RATE
Training a model is a controlled descent down an error surface. The slope tells you which way is downhill; the learning rate tells you how big a step to take; the loop ends when the slope itself goes to zero — not when the error does.

THE LECTURER’S OWN WHY

§ 01 — THE THRESHOLD CONCEPT

What this session exists to flip in your head

State the mental switch once, here, before any mechanism arrives. Everything that follows is in service of this one idea.

THE THRESHOLD CONCEPT

Training a model = an iterative loop that adjusts the model’s parameters by stepping opposite the gradient of an error function, one tiny step at a time. The model stops adjusting when the gradient hits zero — meaning, no matter which way you nudge the parameters, the error doesn’t go down any further. That spot is called the minimum of the error surface. The values of the parameters at the minimum are what we use to make predictions on new data.

The perceptron in this session has only two parameters (m and b) and one input feature (x), so the error surface is a 2D paraboloid — a bowl. The loop walks down to the bottom of the bowl. A deep neural network with 70 billion parameters has a 70-billion-dimensional surface — but the loop and its stopping rule are the same.

The threshold concept lands when you stop thinking of training as “the model gets smarter” and start thinking of it as “a fixed update rule keeps firing until it can’t move the loss any further.” No magic, no understanding — just a derivative-driven walk.

CHECK YOURSELFIf you were told the gradient of the loss with respect to every parameter is exactly zero, what — if anything — should you do next? (Two acceptable answers; one of them is “stop training.”)
§ 02 — THE INSPIRATION

The biological neuron, and its limits as an analogy

The lecturer opens with the standard “ANN was inspired by biological neurons” story and then immediately admits “in real time I don’t find any kind of relation between [the biological] neuron and the math neuron.” That candor is worth preserving — treat the analogy as historical motivation, not as a working model.

A biological neuron has three relevant parts:

  1. Dendrites — branches that receive electrochemical signals from upstream neurons.
  2. Soma (cell body) — sums those signals; if the sum crosses a threshold, the neuron fires.
  3. Axon — sends the resulting signal downstream through synapses to other neurons’ dendrites.
Transcript fix. The lecturer said the neuron has “dendrite, axon, and neuron” — a slip; she said “neuron” twice. The third part is the soma (cell body), and the synapse is the gap between axon and the next dendrite. None of this changes the math, but if you carry the analogy into the next session it’s worth having the names right.

The mathematical version keeps the shape of the picture — many inputs → one summing step → one output — and discards everything else (no chemistry, no membrane potentials, no refractory periods, no actual decision-making). Don’t smuggle “the network thinks” intuitions back in from the biology. The network multiplies, adds, and steps a parameter; that’s the entire mechanism.

FAILURE TELLWhen a colleague says “the model decided X” or “the model understood Y,” they are leaking the biological-neuron analogy into a place it doesn’t belong. The model maximised a scalar score under a fixed update rule. Decision and understanding are not in there.
CHECK YOURSELFName two properties of biological neurons that the mathematical neuron deliberately throws away.
§ 03 — THE PERCEPTRON

A single artificial neuron

A perceptron is a single artificial neuron — one summing step with adjustable weights and a bias, followed by an activation function that decides what to output. The historical perceptron (Rosenblatt, 1958) used a hard step activation — output 1 if the weighted sum exceeded a threshold, otherwise 0 — and learned by a rule called the perceptron learning rule, designed for binary classification.

Correction — date. The lecturer placed the perceptron in 1956. Rosenblatt published it as “The Perceptron: A Probabilistic Model for Information Storage and Organization in the Brain” in 1958 in Psychological Review. 1956 was the Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence — the workshop that coined the term “AI.” The two events are routinely conflated. (Same correction as in Session1-FoundationModels-Opener-changelog.md; carried forward here for the citation chain.)
Disentangle this now — it pays off in Session 4. What the lecturer derives today is not Rosenblatt’s original perceptron. She uses the perceptron’s wiring (inputs → weighted sum → output) but with the identity activation (output = the weighted sum, no step) and mean-squared error as the loss, trained by gradient descent. That combination is linear regression, not Rosenblatt’s binary classifier. Throughout this lesson, treat “perceptron” as the lecturer’s shorthand for “single artificial neuron”, and remember that the activation function is what turns it into one thing or another. Next session adds sigmoid, tanh, and ReLU activations — and the original Rosenblatt perceptron (with its step) returns by name.

The mathematical neuron in this session looks like this:

One input feature x, one weight m, one bias term b, the identity activation. The “training” we’re about to do is finding values of m and b such that ŷ = m · x + b makes good predictions across a dataset.

JAVA / SPRING BRIDGE

Think of the perceptron as a class with two mutable fields and one method:

class Perceptron {
    double m = 5.0;            // weight (initial guess)
    double b = 5.0;            // bias (initial guess)
    double predict(double x) { return m * x + b; }
}

Training is a train(x, y) method that nudges m and b after seeing each (x, y) example. We’ll write that method by the end of §09.

CHECK YOURSELFIn your own words: what is the one thing about the perceptron’s wiring that you have to know to recognise it inside a much bigger neural network?
§ 04 — FROM DATA TO A LINE

Scatter plot → relationship → best-fit line

Setup. Take the lecturer’s example: x = temperature in °C, y = price of an air conditioner. Intuition says when summer heats up, AC prices rise. We want to test that — and, if it holds, to predict AC price given temperature.

TEMPERATURE (x, °C)AC PRICE (y, ₹k) — ILLUSTRATIVE
2532
2632.5
3335
4336
……

A scatter plot is just the dataset drawn as dots — one dot per (x, y) pair, x on the horizontal axis, y on the vertical. If, scanning the scatter, you see that y tends to climb when x climbs (or vice versa), and the climb looks straight-ish, the two are said to have a linear relationship. “Linear” means degree 1 — y = 3x is linear and plots as a straight line; y = 3x² is not linear and plots as a curve.

Once you’ve decided the relationship is roughly linear, the next move is to summarise it with one line — a single line that runs through the cloud of dots in a way that captures the trend. That’s called the best-fit line. “Best” has a precise definition we’ll get to in §06; the intuition is “the line that’s collectively as close as possible to every dot.”

WHY THIS STEP MATTERS

A line is a generic pattern. The dataset has 4 rows above; in production it might have 4 million. You can’t store every row’s deviation and reason about it individually — but you can keep two numbers (the line’s slope and intercept) and use them to predict y for any x you’ve never seen. Compressing the dataset into two numbers is the entire point of training a linear model.

JAVA / SPRING BRIDGE

A Map<Double, Double> from temperature → price would memorise the four rows above but predict nothing for 27°C. The best-fit line is a learned function — Function<Double, Double> price = t -> m*t + b; — that interpolates and extrapolates. The training step’s job is to set m and b.

FAILURE TELLIf the scatter plot has no visible trend — points scattered randomly — a “best-fit line” is meaningless. The optimisation will still find a slope and intercept, but that line tells you nothing useful. Always plot the data first. If x and y aren’t related, a linear model isn’t your tool.
CHECK YOURSELFWhy does the lecturer plot the data before talking about lines? What would go wrong if she skipped that step?
§ 05 — THE LINE EQUATION

y = m·x + b: what’s known and what isn’t

A line in the plane has the equation y = m·x + b, where:

  • m is the slope — how much y rises when x rises by 1.
  • b is the intercept (also called the bias) — the value of y when x = 0. The transcript uses c; the ML world uses b for bias. We’ll use b from here on so the terminology lines up with later sessions and the ANN handout.

In the training data, x is known (the temperatures you observed) and y is known (the AC prices you observed). What you don’t know — and what training has to discover — are m and b. Once you have them, prediction is trivial: take any temperature x, compute ŷ = m·x + b, and that’s your predicted price.

So the whole problem of training reduces to: find the values of m and b that make the line a good fit. Two unknowns, one objective.

HAT NOTATION

ŷ (read: “y-hat”) is the predicted value — what the line says y should be at a given x. Plain y is the actual observed value from the data. The gap ŷ − y is the error for that example.

JAVA / SPRING BRIDGE

Two mutable fields, one read-only input:

double m, b;                          // the unknowns; mutate during training
double predict(double x) { return m * x + b; }   // x is the input

Training is the algorithm that, after seeing many (x, y) examples, leaves m and b at values that minimise the average error across the dataset.

CHECK YOURSELFIf somebody hands you trained values m = 0.18 and b = 27.5 for the AC dataset above, what’s your predicted price at x = 30°C?
§ 06 — ERROR & THE LOSS LANDSCAPE

What “error” means — and the shape of what we’re descending

Per-example error. For a single training row (xᵢ, yᵢ):

errorᵢ = ŷᵢ − yᵢ            where  ŷᵢ = m·xᵢ + b

That’s a signed number. If the line predicted too high, errorᵢ > 0; too low, errorᵢ < 0. If we just summed signed errors across the dataset, positive and negative would cancel and a line that’s wildly wrong but symmetric would look perfect. So we square each error first.

Cost (or loss) over the whole dataset with N training examples:

                  N
J(m, b)  =  1/N · Σ (ŷᵢ − yᵢ)²
                 i=1

This is called the mean-squared error (MSE) — the average squared error across all examples. The handout (page 8) writes the same formula:

LOSS vs. COST — COMMON INTERVIEW QUESTION

Loss = the error from one training example. Cost (or objective, or risk) = the average loss across all examples (or a batch of them). People use the terms interchangeably in practice; you’ll see “loss function” applied to both. The names matter less than knowing which formula you mean.

J(m, b) is a function of two variables. If you fix the dataset and vary m and b, you get a different cost number for every choice. Plot that — height = cost, the two horizontal axes = m and b — and you get a surface. For MSE on a linear model the surface is a paraboloid (a 3D bowl): one global minimum, no other local minima, gently convex everywhere. The whole game is to walk down to the bottom of that bowl.

Correction — the most important one in this session. The lecturer repeats “find m and b such that average error equals 0” throughout the session, including in her one-line summary. This is not the right framing. With MSE on any real (noisy) dataset, the minimum value of J(m, b) is strictly positive — it’s the irreducible noise floor. There is no line that hits every dot, so the squared-error sum is never zero. What is true: the gradient of J(m, b) is zero at the minimum, because at the bottom of a bowl every direction is uphill. The stopping condition is “the gradient is ≈ 0,” not “the error is ≈ 0.” Section §11 makes this operational.
FAILURE TELLIf your loss appears to be heading to exactly 0 during training of a regression model on real-world data, you almost certainly have a bug: a leaked label into the features, a mis-shuffled train/test split, or you’re computing loss on training data the model has already memorised. Real losses bottom out above zero.
CHECK YOURSELFWhy do we square the per-example error before averaging, rather than just taking its absolute value? (Two acceptable answers — one mathematical, one optimisation-friendly.)
§ 07 — THE DIRECTION PROBLEM

Why random guessing of m and b doesn’t converge

So now the picture is concrete: pick (m, b), compute J(m, b), see how big it is. Try a different (m, b), see if J went down or up.

The lecturer walks through what happens if you try to descend the bowl by random guessing: pick m = 5, b = 5, get a big error; pick m = 10, b = 4, see if the error is bigger or smaller; pick m = 3, b = 6; and so on. The problem isn’t that you can’t evaluate the cost — that’s a one-line computation. The problem is direction:

THE LECTURER’S WORDING

“In step 2, what you don’t know is what to do with m and b. You don’t know which direction to go — increase or decrease.”

Random guessing fails for two reasons:

  1. No commitment. Each guess is independent of the last. Even if step 2 is better than step 1, step 3 is just another roll of the dice.
  2. No proportionality. When you’re far from the minimum, you’d want big moves; when you’re close, small ones. Random guesses don’t scale to where you are.

Both problems have the same fix: use the local slope of the cost function to decide both which way to move and (in proportion to its size) how big a step to take. That’s gradient descent. The next two sections build up to it.

CHECK YOURSELFWhy is “I increased m by 1 and the loss dropped” not sufficient to decide what to do with b?
§ 08 — SLOPE = DERIVATIVE = GRADIENT

The directional signal

The lecturer makes a simple, important claim: slope, derivative, and gradient are the same family of concept (the rate-of-change of a function at a point). Three vocabularies — high-school geometry, calculus, and ML — converge here, with one subtlety: the gradient of a multi-variable function is technically a vector (one slope per parameter), while slope and derivative are scalars for single-variable functions. The three terms collapse to the same number when there’s only one parameter to vary.

  • Slope of a line = rise / run = how much y changes per unit change in x.
  • Derivative of a function f(x) at a point a, written df/dx |_{x=a} or f′(a) = the slope of the tangent line to f at a. For a non-straight curve, the slope is different at every point; the derivative gives you the slope at that point.
  • Gradient of a multi-variable function J(m, b), written ∇J = the vector of all partial derivatives (∂J/∂m, ∂J/∂b) — one slope per parameter, packaged together.

The handout (page 2) makes this concrete with two numerical examples:

WHAT THE GRADIENT DOES FOR YOU OPERATIONALLY

At any point (m, b), computing (∂J/∂m, ∂J/∂b) tells you the direction in which J increases fastest, and how steeply. The opposite of that vector — −(∂J/∂m, ∂J/∂b) — is the direction of steepest decrease. Walk a tiny step in that direction and J drops by approximately the gradient’s magnitude times the step size.

FAILURE TELLIf ∂J/∂m is positive at your current spot, the loss rises as m rises — so you should decrease m. If it’s negative, the loss falls as m rises — so you should increase m. The mnemonic is the opposite of the sign of the gradient. The lecturer summarises this as “find the slope, go reverse” — which is the right intuition; the worked example in the transcript that says “go reverse of right-pointing arrow → so increase m” is internally inconsistent. The clean version is in §09 below.
JAVA / SPRING BRIDGE — NEWTON’S METHOD

Most Java developers met Newton-Raphson root-finding in a numerical-methods class: pick x, evaluate f(x), use f′(x) to step toward where f(x) = 0. Gradient descent is the same idea, applied to the derivative of the cost: we want ∂J/∂w = 0, so we step w in the direction that drives ∂J/∂w toward zero. Same family of iterative numerical methods; different use case.

CHECK YOURSELFAt J(m) = m², what does the gradient at m = −3 tell you to do with m to reduce J?
§ 09 — THE UPDATE RULE

Gradient descent in one expression

Now we have everything to write the update. Start with the cost on a single example (SGD form — one example at a time):

J = (ŷ − y)²        where  ŷ = m·x + b

The handout (page 12) does the partial derivatives in plain English:

∂J/∂m  =  ∂/∂m (ŷ − y)²
       =  2 · (ŷ − y) · ∂(ŷ − y)/∂m
       =  2 · (ŷ − y) · ∂(m·x + b − y)/∂m
       =  2 · error · x

∂J/∂b  =  2 · (ŷ − y) · ∂(m·x + b − y)/∂b
       =  2 · error · 1
       =  2 · error

(That’s the chain rule in action — the outer function u² differentiates to 2u, and the inner (m·x + b − y) differentiates to x for m and 1 for b. We meet the chain rule properly in Session 5 with backpropagation — the same idea applied layer by layer.)

The gradient descent update rule says: subtract a small multiple of the gradient from the current parameter value.

m_new = m_old − η · ∂J/∂m  =  m_old − η · 2 · error · x
b_new = b_old − η · ∂J/∂b  =  b_old − η · 2 · error

η (eta) is the learning rate — a small positive number you choose. Convention absorbs the factor of 2 into η (since η is yours to pick anyway), which is why the handout (page 13) writes:

m_new = m_old − error · x · η
b_new = b_old − error · η
Clarification — full-batch vs SGD. The handout’s formula is the per-example update — stochastic gradient descent (SGD). The full-batch version averages the gradient across all N examples before stepping: 
m_new = m_old − η · (2/N) · Σᵢ (errorᵢ · xᵢ)
b_new = b_old − η · (2/N) · Σᵢ errorᵢ
SGD is faster per step but noisier; full-batch is the opposite. Mini-batch (somewhere in between) is what production systems actually use. The lecturer plans to cover all three in the next session.

Clean worked example — the parabola J(w) = w²

Let η = 0.1. Start at w = 5.

STEPwJ = w²∂J/∂w = 2wUPDATE: w − η·∂J/∂w
05.00025.00010.0005 − 0.1·10 = 4.000
14.00016.0008.0004 − 0.1·8 = 3.200
23.20010.2406.4003.2 − 0.1·6.4 = 2.560
32.5606.5545.1202.56 − 0.1·5.12 = 2.048
……………
∞0.0000.0000.000(already at minimum)

Two things to notice in the table and the diagram:

  1. The sign of ∂J/∂w is positive at every step (we’re on the right half of the parabola) — and the update subtracts that positive number, so w decreases at every step. The rule moves us toward the minimum at w = 0.
  2. The size of the step shrinks as we approach the minimum, because ∂J/∂w = 2w itself shrinks as w shrinks. Gradient descent automatically takes smaller steps near the bottom — without you having to schedule it.
FAILURE TELLIf η is too large, the step at w = 5 would overshoot zero and land at, say, w = −7; the next gradient is now −14; the next step is −7 − 0.1·(−14) = −5.6; the loop bounces around and may diverge (loss grows without bound). If η is too small, the loss decreases by tiny fractions per epoch and training takes thousands of unnecessary iterations. Tuning η is the central knob.
JAVA / SPRING BRIDGE — THE FULL train METHOD
class Perceptron {
    double m = 5.0, b = 5.0;
    double eta = 0.01;

    double predict(double x) { return m * x + b; }

    void train(double x, double y) {       // SGD: one example
        double yHat = predict(x);
        double error = yHat - y;            // (ŷ − y), signed
        m -= eta * error * x;               // the handout’s m_new line
        b -= eta * error;                   // the handout’s b_new line
    }
}

That’s the whole training algorithm for a perceptron. Five lines. The rest of the course is what to add when this isn’t enough.

CHECK YOURSELFRun one step of the clean parabola example by hand, but starting at w = −5 (the left half of the parabola). What’s the sign of ∂J/∂w, and which direction does w move?
§ 10 — THE STEP-SIZE KNOB

Learning rate η

The learning rate is the single most important hyperparameter in deep learning. It controls how big a step the update rule takes. The lecturer’s central observation:

THE LECTURER’S RULE OF THUMB

“When you are far away, take big steps. When you are near, take baby steps.”

Gradient descent on a convex bowl does the near part for you automatically — the gradient itself shrinks near the minimum. But the overall scale of every step is η, and that scale is yours to choose.

η CHOICEWHAT HAPPENSHOW YOU’D CATCH IT
Far too small (η = 10⁻⁹)Loss decreases by invisible amounts per epochTraining “doesn’t seem to be doing anything”; loss curve looks flat on a normal scale
Slightly too small (η = 10⁻⁵)Converges, but takes 100× more epochs than necessaryCompare wall-clock against a known-good setting; loss curve takes forever to plateau
Sweet spotLoss drops steeply at first, then asymptotes near the minimumThe standard “elbow” loss curve
Slightly too largeLoss decreases but oscillates around the minimumLoss curve is jagged, doesn’t fully stabilise
Far too largeLoss increases and may blow up to ∞ or NaNLoss curve goes the wrong way; later iterations produce NaN gradients

Worked-example sensitivity to η. The handout (page 13) shows what happens if you naively crank η up. With m_old = 500, error = 5, x = 2:

  • η = 3:  m_new = 500 − 5·2·3 = 470 (step size 30)
  • η = 6:  m_new = 500 − 5·2·6 = 440 (step size 60)
  • η = 10: m_new = 500 − 5·2·10 = 400 (step size 100)

Bigger η ⇒ bigger jump. That’s it. The danger of cranking it too high isn’t visible in one step; it shows up when the next gradient points the other way and you’ve already leapt past the minimum.

PRODUCTION PRACTICE (CONTEXT, NOT EXAM)

Modern training rarely uses a fixed η. Learning-rate schedules (warm-up + cosine decay), adaptive optimisers (Adam, AdamW), and per-parameter rates all aim at the same thing: take big steps where it’s safe, small steps where it isn’t, without you having to find the magic constant by trial and error. The vanilla rate-tuning we’re doing today is what those methods are built on top of.

FAILURE TELLLoss curve goes up after the first few epochs → η is too large. Cut it by 10× and re-run. (Or by 3×, if you want to be gentle.) This is the first thing to try, always.
CHECK YOURSELFTwo trained models report final losses of 0.04 and 0.08 respectively. Without seeing their loss curves, what does that comparison alone not tell you?
§ 11 — STOPPING

The stopping condition (and why it’s the gradient, not the error)

The lecturer’s final summary says: “Whenever you get error = 0, the whole [update] term will be 0, so m_new = m_old and you stop. That’s the optimal value.”

The arithmetic is correct in the lecturer’s formula — if error = 0 exactly for the current example, the update term η · error · x is zero and nothing changes. But on real data, error = 0 for every example is not achievable unless your line passes through every dot (which never happens on noisy real data). The stopping condition that actually fires in practice is one of:

  1. The gradient magnitude is below a tolerance, e.g. ‖∇J‖ < 10⁻⁶. The intuition: the surface is flat enough that further steps wouldn’t move us meaningfully.
  2. The change in loss between epochs drops below a tolerance, e.g. J_prev − J_now < 10⁻⁵. The intuition: we’re plateaued; the loss has stopped meaningfully decreasing.
  3. A fixed maximum number of epochs is hit. A safety net. Most training scripts have both (2) and (3).
  4. Validation loss starts rising while training loss keeps falling. That’s overfitting; stop here. (This is “early stopping” — Session ≥ 5.)
WHY THIS MATTERS

“Train until loss = 0” sounds like a clean instruction, but it’s wrong, and trying to enforce it ends in one of three places:

  • Your loss can hit zero — you’ve leaked the labels into the features, or you’re computing loss on the training data after the model has memorised it.
  • Your loss never moves — η is too small or the problem genuinely has no signal.
  • Training runs forever — there’s no stopping rule, and the gradient is still small-but-nonzero.

Bigger landscape, briefly. A 2D parabola has exactly one minimum and gradient descent always finds it. A deep neural network’s loss landscape is non-convex — it has many local minima, saddle points (flat in some directions, downhill in others), and ridges. Vanilla gradient descent can stall on saddle points or get stuck in a poor local minimum. The fixes — momentum, Adam, learning-rate scheduling, better initialisation — are the next few sessions. For today, take comfort: linear regression’s loss landscape is the easy case.

FAILURE TELLLoss decreases for a while and then plateaus at a number that seems too high. Three things to check, in order: (i) is η too small to climb out of the plateau? (ii) are you at a real minimum and that’s just the irreducible error on this data? (iii) is the model too simple for the relationship — should y = m·x + b actually be y = m·x² + …?
CHECK YOURSELFWhy is “stop when validation loss starts rising” a better stopping rule than “stop when training loss is below a tolerance”?
§ 12 — MORE FEATURES

Multi-feature linear regression

So far: one input feature x, two parameters m and b. Real datasets have many features — temperature, humidity, day of week, time of day, festival or not, retailer chain, postcode. The model extends in the obvious way:

ŷ = w₁·x₁ + w₂·x₂ + … + wₙ·xₙ + b

— n weights (one per feature, called w₁, …, wₙ instead of m) and one shared bias b.

Correction — bias per feature. The lecturer wrote the multi-feature form as m₁x₁ + b₁ + m₂x₂ + b₂ + m₃x₃ + b₃ = y — with one bias per feature. That’s not how it works. There is one bias term b, added once at the end. (Adding multiple biases is mathematically harmless — they’d just collapse into a single effective bias during training — but it’s the wrong form to teach because it suggests features are independent of each other, which they’re not.)
Correction — training process. The lecturer described multi-feature training as “solve one input at a time, keeping all other inputs constant.” That’s a description of a partial derivative — what ∂J/∂w₁ means — not how the algorithm actually runs. In practice, every weight updates simultaneously on each iteration. The chain of updates is: 
for each example (x₁, …, xₙ, y):
    ŷ      = w₁·x₁ + … + wₙ·xₙ + b
    error  = ŷ − y
    w₁    -= η · error · x₁          ┓
    w₂    -= η · error · x₂          │ all in parallel,
     ⋮                              │ in the same step
    wₙ    -= η · error · xₙ          ┛
    b     -= η · error
Notice each weight’s update uses the same shared error — the only thing that varies across wᵢ is xᵢ, the input that weight is responsible for.
JAVA / SPRING BRIDGE — THE GENERALISATION
class LinearModel {
    double[] w;             // one weight per feature
    double b;
    double eta = 0.01;

    double predict(double[] x) {
        double sum = b;
        for (int i = 0; i < w.length; i++) sum += w[i] * x[i];
        return sum;
    }

    void train(double[] x, double y) {
        double yHat = predict(x);
        double error = yHat - y;
        for (int i = 0; i < w.length; i++) w[i] -= eta * error * x[i];
        b -= eta * error;
    }
}

Same shape as the single-feature version. The for loop over weights is doing what the lecturer was hand-waving as “for every column.”

CHECK YOURSELFThree features. After computing one prediction and one error on example (x₁, x₂, x₃, y), how many parameters get updated, and by how many distinct signed error values?
§ 13 — THE FORWARD LINK

Where this loop reappears inside a Transformer

The lecturer’s closing argument: “Transformers are built on top of these algorithms. One block of a Transformer is an ANN. So this isn’t optional — it’s the foundation.”

Concretely, a single Transformer encoder block (Session 7) contains a feed-forward network layer that is, mechanically:

FFN(x) = max(0, x·W₁ + b₁) · W₂ + b₂

That’s two stacked linear regressions (the x·W + b shape we just derived) with a ReLU activation (max(0, ·)) wedged between them. Inside, every entry of W₁, W₂, b₁, b₂ is trained by the same gradient-descent update rule you wrote in §09 — just generalised to many parameters, computed in batches, with the chain rule applied through the activation. The optimiser is usually Adam instead of vanilla SGD, but Adam is gradient descent with per-parameter adaptive learning rates (second-moment scaling, à la RMSProp) and a momentum-like first-moment term bolted on (Kingma & Ba 2014). The base loop — predict, compute error, take a step opposite the gradient — is unchanged.

So when you read the Transformer paper and see “trained with Adam on the WMT dataset for 100,000 steps” — what’s happening at every one of those steps is the loop from this session, scaled to billions of parameters.

WHAT’S NEXT

Session 4 introduces the activation functions (step, sigmoid, tanh, ReLU) that the perceptron’s identity activation has been standing in for. Once activations are in the picture, a single layer of artificial neurons becomes a non-linear model — and stacking layers becomes a deep network. Session 5 covers backpropagation — applying the chain rule through stacked layers, which is the missing piece needed to train the deep network with the same gradient-descent loop. The gradient-descent loop you built today carries forward unchanged; only the activation, the chain rule’s complexity, and the optimiser get fancier.

CHECK YOURSELFWithout re-reading, recite the update rule for m and b from memory. Then check it against §09. If you can’t, this session isn’t done with you.
§ 14 — DIAGNOSTIC TABLE

Symptom → cause → fix

SYMPTOMLIKELY CAUSEFIX
Loss explodes to ∞ or becomes NaNLearning rate too large; updates overshoot and land further uphillCut η by 10× and retry
Loss decreases then plateaus high above zeroAt the global minimum of a noisy problem (which isn’t 0), or stuck in a flat regionDon’t assume 0 is reachable; check on a holdout set; if loss is still poor, switch to a non-linear model
Loss decreases vanishingly slowlyLearning rate too smallIncrease η (or use an adaptive optimiser — Adam, covered later)
Loss decreases on training data but rises on validationOverfittingAdd data; regularise; stop earlier (early stopping)
Loss exactly zero on training dataEither trivially-easy synthetic data, or labels leaked into features. The second is a bug.Audit the feature pipeline; recheck train/validation split
First-step gradient is exactly zeroAll weights initialised to the same value (symmetry); or all features have variance zeroSmall random initialisation; sanity-check feature variance
Loss curve oscillates without settlingη slightly too large for the late-stage stepsDecay η over the course of training (LR schedule), or use Adam
Best-fit line predicts the opposite trend in two runsx and y have no real linear relationshipPlot the scatter; switch model or accept the conclusion
§ 15 — QUIZ YOURSELF

Ten questions

Recall

  1. State the perceptron’s prediction formula and the gradient-descent update for m and b.
  2. What is the difference between loss and cost?
  3. Why is “average error = 0” not the right stopping condition for training on real data?

Application

  1. You’re handed a dataset with 1,000 rows of (temperature, ac_price). You start training with m = 0, b = 0, η = 0.001. After 50 epochs your loss has barely moved. What’s the first thing you try?
  2. Same dataset, but η = 10. The loss blows up to infinity in 3 epochs. What do you change?
  3. You’ve got a perceptron and want to add a second feature — humidity. Sketch the new prediction formula and the update rule for the new weight.
  4. Your loss has decreased smoothly to 0.04 on training data and is sitting at 0.27 on a held-out validation set. Diagnose.

Debugging

  1. Training reports loss = 0.0 on the very first epoch. Are you done? (No. What’s the actual diagnosis?)
  2. Training loss is decreasing reliably on each epoch but ∂J/∂m is increasing in magnitude. What’s going on geometrically?
  3. Plain-English chain. For one example (x = 30, y = 35) with current (m = 1, b = 5, η = 0.01): what did we predict? How wrong were we? Whose fault is it (m, b, or both)? What does the update rule do about it?
ANSWERS
  1. ŷ = m·x + b. m_new = m_old − η·error·x, b_new = b_old − η·error, where error = ŷ − y.
  2. Loss is the error from one example; cost is the average loss over the dataset (or a batch).
  3. Real data has irreducible noise; the minimum of MSE is strictly positive. If you reach exactly zero, you’ve either memorised the training set (and will fail on new data) or leaked labels into features.
  4. Increase η. The training is alive but moving too slowly.
  5. Decrease η. Start by cutting it 10× and see if training stabilises.
  6. ŷ = w_t · temperature + w_h · humidity + b. Update: w_t -= η · error · temperature, w_h -= η · error · humidity, b -= η · error. Same shared error for all three updates.
  7. Overfitting. Add more data, add regularisation, or stop training earlier (the gap between train and validation loss is the tell).
  8. Almost certainly a bug — either the labels are in the features, the loss isn’t connected to the labels, or the optimiser isn’t actually stepping. Print a few (ŷ, y) pairs and check whether the predictions equal the labels by coincidence or by mechanism.
  9. You’re moving away from the minimum. Likely cause: η is large enough that the previous step overshot, and you’re now on the other side and steeper.
  10. Predict: ŷ = 1·30 + 5 = 35. Error: 35 − 35 = 0. Whose fault: nobody — this example happens to be exactly on the current line. Update: zero change. (This is the perceptron’s pleasant surprise: when the line already fits this example, the update is automatically a no-op. The point of SGD is that the next example will probably not fit and will move the parameters.)

§ 16 — GLOSSARY

The vocabulary of this session

ANN (artificial neural network)
A network of artificial neurons (perceptrons with activations), each of which sums its weighted inputs and applies an activation function before passing its output to the next layer.
Best-fit line
The line that minimises a chosen error measure (here: mean-squared error) across all data points. Two parameters: slope and intercept.
Bias term b
The additive constant in ŷ = m·x + b. Lets the line cross the y-axis at any point. (Also called intercept in plain-stats land; called bias in ML.)
Cost
Average loss over a dataset or batch.
Convergence
The state where further iterations of training change the parameters by less than a chosen tolerance. The training loop ends here.
Derivative
The slope of a function at a point. For straight lines, constant; for curves, different at each point.
Epoch
One full pass through every training example. (Definition handed off from the handout; the lecturer will define it formally next session along with batch and iteration.)
Error (per example)
ŷ − y. Signed.
Feature (X)
An input variable to the model. Temperature, humidity, time of day, etc.
Gradient ∇J
The vector of partial derivatives of a multi-variable function, one entry per parameter. Points in the direction of steepest increase.
Gradient descent
The iterative algorithm that subtracts the gradient (times η) from the parameters at each step, walking the parameters toward a minimum of the cost.
Identity activation
Output equals input. A perceptron with identity activation and MSE loss is linear regression.
Learning rate η
The multiplier on the gradient in the update rule. Sets the step size.
Linear regression
A linear model (ŷ = w·x + b) trained by minimising MSE (usually via gradient descent or closed-form normal equations).
Loss
Error from a single training example.
Loss landscape
The surface formed by plotting the cost as a function of all the model’s parameters. For linear regression with MSE, this is a paraboloid (convex).
Mean-squared error (MSE)
(1/N)·Σ(ŷᵢ − yᵢ)². The standard cost for regression.
Minimum, global
The point on the loss landscape with the lowest cost value. For convex losses (like MSE on linear regression), the only minimum and what gradient descent finds.
Minimum, local
A point that is lower than all its neighbours but higher than the global minimum. Vanilla gradient descent can get stuck in one (not a worry for MSE-on-linear; very much a worry in deep networks).
Partial derivative ∂J/∂m
The derivative of J with respect to m, treating all other parameters as constants. One component of the gradient.
Perceptron
A single artificial neuron: weighted sum of inputs plus a bias, run through an activation. Historical (Rosenblatt 1958) used a step activation; the lecturer’s “perceptron” today uses the identity activation, making it linear regression.
Prediction (ŷ, “y-hat”)
What the model outputs given an input.
Scatter plot
A 2D plot of (x, y) pairs as dots; the first move before reasoning about relationships.
Slope
Same as the derivative for a single-variable function. The rate of change.
SGD (stochastic gradient descent)
Gradient descent that updates after every single training example, instead of waiting to average over the whole dataset. What the lecturer’s per-example update rule actually is.
Supervised learning
A setting where every training example comes with a known answer (y), so the model can compute an error and correct itself. The opposite is unsupervised, where you only have x.
Target (y)
The answer the model is trying to predict. Also: label, response variable, dependent variable.
Update rule
The equation that produces the next-step parameter from the current-step parameter. For us: param -= η · ∂J/∂param.
Weight (w or m)
The multiplier on an input feature. Tells the model how much that feature should affect the prediction.
